{"claims": [
{"id": "c1", "text": "Circuits returned under specifications that differ only in defensible analytic choices are almost disjoint in their edges. Structural overlap must be read against chance, and it is not the quantity a filing depends on.", "methods": ["Pre-registered crossed multiverse grid over seven analytic axes, every level taken from a published implementation", "Structural comparison of edge sets in GPT-2 small's factorised graph (tens of thousands of edges)"], "results": ["Circuits are almost disjoint (Section 7.1)", "Random subsets of a few hundred edges are expected to share almost nothing, so beating chance overlap is a weak bar"], "conditions": ["GPT-2 small, IOI task", "Structural difference need not imply functional or statement difference"]},
{"id": "c2", "text": "When circuits are mapped through a fixed deterministic claim map to Annex IV / Article 86-style statements, the claim flips on about three quarters of specification pairs. The flips include substantive disagreement about which region of the network is responsible, even at the coarsest granularity.", "methods": ["Deterministic claim map from circuit to natural-language statement, not a language model", "Two addressees: the overseer (where the behaviour is carried and how concentrated it is) and the affected person (which input parts drove the decision)", "Nested granularities", "Specification curve presentation"], "results": ["Claim flips on three quarters of pairs (Section 7.2)"], "conditions": ["The claim map is fixed in advance", "Discretisations such as size categories come from a committed calibration rule"]},
{"id": "c3", "text": "No single analytic axis rescues the filing. Holding any one axis fixed does not remove the disagreement, and the axes that govern structure need not be those that govern statements.", "methods": ["Holding each axis fixed in turn and comparing within its levels"], "results": ["No analytic axis rescues the filing (Section 7.3)", "Standardising the metric would still leave six axes free"], "conditions": ["Standardisation decisions should be made at the level of the statement"]},
{"id": "c4", "text": "Disagreement persists under maximum pressure. With size-dependent content removed from the statement and only same-size circuits compared, attribution of the behaviour to a region still varies.", "methods": ["Size-matched comparison with the statement reduced to region attribution, the core of an Annex IV 2(b) account"], "results": ["The result holds under maximum pressure (Section 7.4), so the disagreement cannot be attributed to the size channel"], "conditions": ["Circuit size is an outcome chosen by the threshold rule, not an axis"]},
{"id": "c5", "text": "Pooled comparisons against a size-matched random baseline mislead, so within-size comparison is required. Circuit size is a hidden channel in multiverse designs.", "methods": ["Random edge subsets of matched size passed through the same claim map", "Within-size decomposition"], "results": ["At large sizes a uniform random draw touches every component and can support only one statement", "A pooled direction can point either way for reasons unrelated to discovery quality"], "conditions": ["A pooled baseline result reported without its within-size counterpart is uninterpretable"]},
{"id": "c6", "text": "Over part of the size range, filings differ more than mechanisms do. This is assessed by chance-corrected, example-level functional agreement, which addresses the phantom specialisation objection.", "methods": ["Example-by-example success/failure agreement using the measures of Bayat Makou et al.", "Cohen's kappa to correct for agreement expected from accuracy alone"], "results": ["Statement disagreement exceeds functional disagreement over part of the range (Section 7.6)"], "conditions": ["Where mechanisms differ more than statements, the procedure is coarser than the mechanisms; where statements differ more, it amplifies differences", "The relationship varies with size"]},
{"id": "c7", "text": "A five-item filability disclosure protocol is implementable without the regulator adjudicating which analytic choice is correct.", "methods": ["Declare the specification space with citations", "Publish the claim map as deterministic code", "State the chosen specification and why it was selected", "Report discard rates per axis level", "Report pooled statistics with their within-group (within-size) decomposition"], "results": ["Satisfiable with existing tooling", "Cheap relative to the sweep that produced the circuit"], "conditions": ["Covers what a careful paper should already report"]},
{"id": "c8", "text": "The design is pre-registered and bounded by the library. Its conclusions are conservative relative to the literature and are limited to one model and one task.", "methods": ["Grid of 7 objectives x 7 operators x 4 corruptions nested in 5 operators x 4 metrics x 3 thresholds x 2 prompt variants x 5 seeds = 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 specifications", "Discards recorded, not repaired", "Bootstrap over specifications, not pairs", "Pre-registered Pythia-160m replication of 924 cells with 3 seeds"], "results": ["Optimal ablation is not in the library and is therefore excluded", "343 tests; numeric tokens verified against stored outputs"], "conditions": ["The seed selects sampled prompts and so measures evaluation-set variability, not nondeterminism", "Bootstrap is unreliable for small groups", "Nothing is claimed about scale", "A second task is designed but not run"]}
],
"items": [
{"id": "q1", "type": "why", "claims": ["c8"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does the grid contain 1,540 discovery cells but 18,480 specifications?", "answer": "The metric (4 levels) and threshold (3 levels) are applied to a circuit after discovery rather than changing the discovery run. Each discovery cell (objective x operator/corruption combination x prompt x seed = 7 x 22 x 2 x 5) therefore yields 4 x 3 = 12 specifications.", "rubric": ["States that each discovery cell yields 12 specifications (18,480 = 1,540 x 12)", "Attributes the factor of 12 to the 4 metrics x 3 thresholds applied after discovery"]},
{"id": "q2", "type": "why", "claims": ["c8"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does the pre-registered Pythia-160m replication have 924 cells?", "answer": "The objective x operator/corruption combinations give 7 x (2 + 5 x 4) = 154, and the 2 prompt variants double this to 308. With only 3 seeds instead of 5, that gives 924 discovery cells, i.e. 1,540 x 3/5.", "rubric": ["Identifies the seed axis reduction from 5 to 3 as the only difference", "Shows the arithmetic: 154 x 2 x 3 = 924, or equivalently 1,540 x 3/5"]},
{"id": "q3", "type": "why", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose discovered circuits in some part of the grid are mostly large. Why could a pooled random-baseline comparison make them look less statement-stable than random subgraphs, even if discovery is sound?", "answer": "At large sizes a random draw touches every component and can support only one statement, so random pairs agree perfectly there while discovered circuits can still vary. Pooling across sizes then favours the random baseline for reasons unrelated to discovery quality.", "rubric": ["Says random large draws all yield the same single statement, so their agreement is trivially high", "Says the pooled comparison mixes size distributions, so the apparent inferiority reflects size rather than discovery quality"]},
{"id": "q4", "type": "why", "claims": ["c8", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does drawing every level from the Miller et al. library make the paper's instability findings hard to dismiss as the product of unreasonable settings?", "answer": "Every level is one the tool's own authors expose as a usable configuration, and none was invented for the study. A critic therefore cannot say the varied choices are indefensible without criticising the tooling's own definitions.", "rubric": ["States that the levels are published or exposed by the tool itself rather than invented", "Concludes that any disagreement arises among choices that count as defensible by the tooling's own standards"]},
{"id": "q5", "type": "why", "claims": ["c8", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Why would repairing cells that fail to execute undermine the study, given what the study is testing?", "answer": "The library is the instrument under test, so repairs would alter the instrument and introduce post-hoc analytic choices. That is exactly the undisclosed flexibility the paper is warning about. Recording discards with their rates keeps the evidence's composition visible instead.", "rubric": ["Notes that repairing changes the instrument under test", "Notes that post-hoc repair is itself analytic flexibility that could shape results, so discards should be recorded and reported instead"]},
{"id": "q6", "type": "why", "claims": ["c2", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "Why is the flip in which region is held responsible problematic for the Article 86 addressee, and not only for the overseer?", "answer": "The coarsest statement available rests on undisclosed choices, and finer statements refine the coarse one rather than replacing it. A flip at the region level therefore propagates to every granularity, including the one offered to an affected person.", "rubric": ["States that the disagreement occurs even at the coarsest granularity", "Explains that nested, finer statements refine the coarse one, so no addressee's account escapes the flip"]},
{"id": "q7", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c8"], "pair": null, "question": "Within-axis conditioning groups in the Pythia-160m replication will be smaller than in the GPT-2 grid. Would bootstrap intervals for those within-group quantities be more or less trustworthy, and what should be reported instead?", "answer": "They would be less trustworthy. With 3 seeds instead of 5, each conditioning group holds fewer specifications, and the paper says bootstrap fails for small groups. Point estimates with diagnostics should be reported instead.", "rubric": ["Says less trustworthy", "Links this to fewer specifications per group (3 seeds vs 5) and the paper's small-group bootstrap limitation", "Recommends point estimates with diagnostics"]},
{"id": "q8", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c2", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "If the claim map had used a language model to write statements, could the three-quarters claim-flip rate still be read as evidence about circuit variation? Why?", "answer": "No. Model variance in statement generation would add to circuit variance, with no way to separate the two, so the flip rate could partly reflect the language model rather than the circuits.", "rubric": ["Says no, the flip rate would no longer be attributable to circuits", "Explains that language-model variance confounds circuit variance and cannot be separated from it"]},
{"id": "q9", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c4", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose the threshold rule gave every metric's circuits a distinct, non-overlapping size band. What could the size-matched control in Section 7.4 then fail to test?", "answer": "Same-size pairs would only ever share a metric, so the control could not test whether changing the metric flips region attribution. Metric effects would be confounded with size and left unexamined.", "rubric": ["Says cross-metric disagreement would go untested under the size-matched control", "Explains that size-matched pairs would all share a metric because size is an outcome tied to the metric"]},
{"id": "q10", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Two circuits each succeed on nearly every IOI prompt and agree on most examples. Would that raw agreement show that they implement the same mechanism?", "answer": "No. With both near-perfect accuracy, high agreement is expected by chance alone. Only chance-corrected agreement such as Cohen's kappa can separate the same mechanism from mere similar accuracy.", "rubric": ["Says no", "Explains that high accuracy produces high raw agreement by chance, so a chance-corrected measure such as kappa is needed"]},
{"id": "q11", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c8", "c2", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "If the metric-relative threshold rule discarded most specifications under one metric, would the pooled claim-flip rate still describe the balanced design? Why?", "answer": "No. The surviving pool would under-represent that metric, so the pooled rate would mainly reflect the other metrics. This is why discard rates per axis level must be reported.", "rubric": ["Says no", "Explains that the surviving pool's composition departs from the balanced grid, so per-level discard rates must be reported"]},
{"id": "q12", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "In the large-size region, discovered circuits show lower statement agreement than random subsets. Would that imply discovery performs worse than random there?", "answer": "No. The random baseline is degenerate there: every draw touches every component and supports the same one statement. The baseline's perfect agreement says nothing about discovery quality.", "rubric": ["Says no", "Explains that the baseline is degenerate at large sizes, supporting only one statement"]},
{"id": "q13", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": null, "question": "If discovered circuits shared clearly more edges than chance, would that establish that their filed statements are compatible?", "answer": "No. Exceeding chance overlap is a weak bar in a graph this large. Circuits with considerable overlap may still support different statements, because filings depend on statements, not edges.", "rubric": ["Says no", "Cites both reasons: beating chance is a weak bar, and structural overlap is not the quantity the statement depends on"]},
{"id": "q14", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c8"], "pair": "p1", "question": "Would adding a fifth evaluation metric to the grid require running any new discovery cells?", "answer": "No. Metrics are applied to already-discovered circuits; specifications go from 1,540 x 12 to 1,540 x 15 while the 1,540 discovery cells stay the same.", "rubric": ["Says no new discovery cells are needed", "Explains that the metric is applied after discovery (the 1,540 vs 18,480 structure)"]},
{"id": "q15", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c8"], "pair": "p1", "question": "Would adding a sixth seed to the grid require running new discovery cells?", "answer": "Yes. The seed selects the sampled prompts that discovery runs on, so it is part of the discovery cell. It would add 308 new cells (7 x 22 x 2).", "rubric": ["Says yes", "Explains that the seed is a discovery-cell axis (prompt sampling), adding 308 cells"]},
{"id": "q16", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c8"], "pair": "p2", "question": "Would adding an eighth ablation operator that never reads the corrupt distribution add exactly 70 discovery cells?", "answer": "Yes. Such an operator is not crossed with the corruptions, so it adds 7 objectives x 2 prompts x 5 seeds = 70 cells.", "rubric": ["Says yes, 70", "Explains that it is not crossed with the 4 corruption levels, being like the two existing non-reading operators"]},
{"id": "q17", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c8"], "pair": "p2", "question": "Would adding an eighth ablation operator that does read the corrupt distribution add exactly 70 discovery cells?", "answer": "No. It would be crossed with the 4 corruption levels, adding 7 x 4 x 2 x 5 = 280 cells.", "rubric": ["Says no", "Explains nesting of the 4 corruptions under corruption-reading operators, giving 280"]},
{"id": "q18", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4"], "pair": "p3", "question": "If region attribution still disagreed across size-matched specifications with size removed from the statement, could the disagreement be attributed to the size channel?", "answer": "No. Size has been held fixed and removed from the statement, so persisting disagreement must come through some other channel.", "rubric": ["Says no", "Explains that the control eliminates size as the route of disagreement"]},
{"id": "q19", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c4", "c5"], "pair": "p3", "question": "If region attribution agreed across size-matched specifications once size was removed from the statement, would the size channel be implicated in the overall claim flips?", "answer": "Yes. The pooled flips would then be explained by analytic choices changing circuit size, which the paper identifies as a hidden channel.", "rubric": ["Says yes", "Explains that disagreement vanishing under size control points to size as the propagating channel"]},
{"id": "q20", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": "p4", "question": "In a size range where statement disagreement exceeds chance-corrected functional disagreement, is the claim map under-reporting the differences between mechanisms?", "answer": "No. There it is amplifying differences the mechanisms do not carry, which is the regime the paper labels 'filings differ more than mechanisms'.", "rubric": ["Says no; the map amplifies rather than under-reports", "Ties this to statements differing more than kappa-based functional disagreement"]},
{"id": "q21", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": "p4", "question": "In a size range where chance-corrected functional disagreement exceeds statement disagreement, is the claim map under-reporting the differences between mechanisms?", "answer": "Yes. The statement procedure is coarser than the mechanisms there, so distinct mechanisms get compatible statements.", "rubric": ["Says yes", "Explains that the procedure is coarser than the mechanisms in that regime"]},
{"id": "q22", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "A provider files a single circuit with its config and a pooled faithfulness score, and nothing else. Which protocol items are still missing?", "answer": "Missing are: the declared specification space with citations (1), the deterministic claim-map code (2), the reason the specification was selected (3, which needs more than the config), per-level discard rates (4), and the within-size decomposition of the pooled score (5).", "rubric": ["Lists the specification space, claim-map code, selection rationale and discard rates as missing", "Notes that the pooled score needs a within-group or within-size decomposition"]},
{"id": "q23", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": null, "question": "A filer is drafting the account owed to a person under Article 86(1). What content should it lead with, and why not the overseer's version?", "answer": "It should lead with which parts of the input drove the decision, because the right is owed to the person the decision concerns. The overseer's account leads with where the behaviour sits and how concentrated it is, which may be inadequate for that person.", "rubric": ["Says it should lead with input segments or input parts that drove the decision", "Contrasts this with the overseer's location and concentration focus, which serves a different addressee"]},
{"id": "q24", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": null, "question": "A conformity body proposes mandating a single faithfulness metric for all circuit filings. Given the paper's results, should it expect filed statements to become compatible?", "answer": "No. No single axis rescues the filing, and six axes would remain free. The axis that changes statements most need not be the metric, so any standard should be checked at the statement level.", "rubric": ["Says no or not necessarily", "Cites the 'no axis rescues' result or the six remaining free axes", "Notes that standardisation should be evaluated at the statement level"]},
{"id": "q25", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "A neuroscience multiverse study selects brain-region clusters by a significance threshold, so cluster size varies by specification. What does this paper recommend for its pooled statistics?", "answer": "Report every pooled statistic with its within-size decomposition. Size is an outcome of the threshold rather than an axis, so it can carry analytic choices into the results as a hidden channel.", "rubric": ["Recommends within-size decomposition of pooled statistics", "Explains that size is a threshold-determined outcome acting as a hidden channel"]},
{"id": "q26", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c8"], "pair": null, "question": "An analyst finds a within-group bootstrap interval for a three-specification group embarrassingly wide. What should they do under the paper's principles?", "answer": "They should report the point estimate with diagnostics. They should not construct a bias-corrected estimator in response to the unwelcome interval, because that would be the analytic flexibility the paper warns against.", "rubric": ["Says to report a point estimate with diagnostics", "Says not to devise a new estimator post hoc, because that is undisclosed flexibility"]},
{"id": "q27", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c8", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "A team reruns the design with a library that also implements optimal ablation. Should they expect a narrower or wider space of filed statements than the GPT-2 grid, and why?", "answer": "Wider, or at least no narrower. An additional defensible operator expands the space, which is why the paper calls its library-bounded conclusions conservative.", "rubric": ["Says wider or at least as wide", "Explains that an added defensible level expands the space, consistent with the 'conservative' framing"]},
{"id": "q28", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c8", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "A provider of a 70B-parameter system wants to cite the three-quarters flip rate as its expected instability. Is that justified?", "answer": "No. The study covers one small model on one task, and the paper says it is not obvious in which direction a larger circuit and statement space would move the result. The provider would need its own declared multiverse.", "rubric": ["Says not justified", "Explains that the result is limited to one model and one task and that the direction of scale effects is untested"]},
{"id": "q29", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c4", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "If region attribution had agreed in the size-matched, size-removed comparison, which conclusion about Annex IV 2(b) accounts would lose its support?", "answer": "The conclusion that even the size-independent core of a general-logic account, namely where in the model the behaviour is located, varies across defensible specifications. The flips could instead be traced to the size channel.", "rubric": ["Identifies the persistence-under-maximum-pressure conclusion about region attribution", "Notes that the disagreement would be attributable to size instead"]},
{"id": "q30", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c3", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "If holding one axis fixed had reduced claim flips to near zero, which conclusion would be undermined, and what would it imply for regulators?", "answer": "The 'no analytic axis rescues the filing' result would be undermined. Standardising that one axis would become a viable route, reducing the need for full specification-space disclosure.", "rubric": ["Identifies the 'no axis rescues' result", "Notes that single-axis standardisation would become viable"]},
{"id": "q31", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c1", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "If circuits had shared most of their edges across specifications, would the claim-flip result automatically lose support?", "answer": "No. Structural overlap and statement compatibility are distinct, and overlapping circuits may still support different statements. Only the structural premise (c1) would change.", "rubric": ["Says no", "Explains that structure and statements are distinct units of analysis"]},
{"id": "q32", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c6", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "If chance-corrected functional agreement had been high across the whole size range while statements still flipped, how would the reading of the claim-flip result change?", "answer": "The phantom specialisation objection would gain ground: the circuits would share a mechanism. The flips would then reflect the claim map amplifying differences everywhere, rather than discovery returning different mechanisms over part of the range.", "rubric": ["Says the flips would be read as amplification by the statement procedure, or phantom specialisation, rather than mechanism differences", "Notes that the 'over part of the range' finding would become the whole range"]},
{"id": "q33", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c8"], "pair": null, "question": "If the Pythia-160m replication met its pre-registered refutation criteria, which conclusions would it weaken and which would remain?", "answer": "It would weaken any extension of the findings beyond GPT-2 small or to other architectures. The GPT-2 IOI results themselves would stand, since the paper claims nothing beyond one model and one task.", "rubric": ["Says it weakens generalisation to other models or architectures", "Says the GPT-2 IOI findings themselves are not overturned"]},
{"id": "q34", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c2", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "If the specification curve showed each region statement supported only by specifications sharing one particular axis level, which other result would be in tension with that pattern?", "answer": "The 'no analytic axis rescues the filing' result. Statements tied to a single axis level would mean fixing that axis would make statements agree.", "rubric": ["Identifies the 'no axis rescues' result", "Explains that statements tied to one axis level imply single-axis standardisation would work"]},
{"id": "q35", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c5", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Which protocol item exists specifically because of the hazard identified for the random baseline?", "answer": "Item 5: report any pooled statistic with its within-group decomposition, particularly within circuit size. Pooled baseline directions can mislead because of size mixing.", "rubric": ["Identifies item 5 (within-group or within-size decomposition)", "Links it to size-mixing in pooled baseline comparisons"]},
{"id": "q36", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c1", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the near-disjointness of circuits show that circuit discovery fails to recover genuine structure? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. Structurally distinct circuits can implement the same computation, as phantom specialisation shows, and the paper disclaims any bearing on whether discovery recovers genuine structure.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Cites structural difference not implying functional difference, or the paper's explicit disclaimer"]},
{"id": "q37", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c8"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that nondeterminism in discovery algorithms is a main driver of circuit instability? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The seed axis selects sampled prompts, so it measures evaluation-set variability rather than nondeterminism, and it is only one of seven axes.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Explains that the seed captures prompt sampling, not algorithmic nondeterminism"]},
{"id": "q38", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper support excluding interpretability evidence from technical documentation? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Contradicted. The protocol is designed to accompany such evidence with disclosure of its specification space, not to remove it.", "rubric": ["Answers contradicted", "Explains that the remedy is disclosure alongside the evidence, not exclusion"]},
{"id": "q39", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c8", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that claim instability spans the full set of defensible choices in the interpretability literature? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The grid is only as wide as the library; optimal ablation, for example, is excluded. The results are therefore a conservative view, not a census of the literature's space.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Cites the library-bounded grid or the optimal ablation omission"]},
{"id": "q40", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c8"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that the same instability would arise for other tasks on GPT-2 small? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. Only IOI was run; a second task is designed but not run.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled", "Notes that only one task was run and the second task is unrun"]},
{"id": "q41", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that the axis causing the most edge-set variation is the best one to standardise? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Contradicted as a general rule. The axes governing structure need not govern statements, so standardising the most structure-changing axis could leave the statement-changing axis free.", "rubric": ["Answers contradicted, or not supported", "Explains the structure/statement axis mismatch and that standardisation should be judged at the statement level"]}
]}

{"items": [
{"id": "q42", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c2", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose the claim map's size categories were picked by hand after the analyst had looked at the discovered circuits. Would the resulting claim-flip rate still be interpretable as evidence about variation across specifications, and why?", "answer": "No. A hand-picked discretisation is itself an undeclared analytic choice made after seeing the data. The flip rate could then reflect where the analyst drew the category boundaries rather than how circuits vary across specifications. The paper requires categories from a committed calibration rule applied to a measured curve, with sensitivity reported and the discretisation declared in the specification space.", "rubric": ["Asserts the flip rate would no longer be cleanly interpretable (or would be compromised).", "Reason: the hand-picked category boundaries are an undeclared, post-hoc analytic choice that can drive the statements and so the flips.", "Condition/remedy: categories must come from a committed calibration rule, with sensitivity reported and the discretisation declared as part of the specification space."]},
{"id": "q43", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "The paper's warning about the random baseline rests on what happens at large circuit sizes. Would that specific degeneracy still arise in a model whose graph is so large that a size-matched random draw never touches every component, even at the largest admitted sizes?", "answer": "No, not that specific degeneracy. It arises because a random draw that touches every component can support only one statement. If draws never cover all components, random subsets can still map to different statements. The within-size comparison remains the recommended practice, but the reason the baseline collapses at large sizes would not apply.", "rubric": ["Asserts the specific degeneracy would not arise (the baseline would not collapse to a single statement).", "Reason: the degeneracy depends on random draws touching every component, which forces one statement; draws that leave components untouched can still yield varied statements."]},
{"id": "q44", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c8"], "pair": null, "question": "The deviations file records whether each deviation was decided before or after the affected material was seen. If that before/after field were dropped, what protection would the pre-registration lose?", "answer": "Readers could no longer tell whether a change was made in response to results. That would hide exactly the kind of data-dependent analytic flexibility the paper studies. The study's own conclusions could then not be distinguished from flexibility-manufactured ones, and a study about analytic flexibility that was itself flexible would undermine its own argument.", "rubric": ["Asserts readers could no longer distinguish result-driven (post hoc) changes from pre-planned ones.", "Reason: undisclosed post hoc changes are exactly the analytic flexibility the paper warns about, so the study's conclusions could be self-undermining."]},
{"id": "q45", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c2", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose some threshold settings admitted discovered circuits so large that each touched every component. Would high agreement among those circuits' region statements count as evidence of filability, and why?", "answer": "No. A circuit that touches every component maps to a single region statement, just as the large random draw does. Agreement there is forced by the mapping and size rather than by convergent mechanisms. The agreement is degenerate and uninformative about whether competent analysts would reach compatible accounts.", "rubric": ["Asserts the agreement would not be evidence of filability.", "Reason: circuits touching every component can support only one statement, so agreement is guaranteed by size/the mapping (degenerate), as with the large-size random baseline."]},
{"id": "q46", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c8", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose the pool of IOI prompts the seed axis samples from were so small that different seeds drew nearly identical prompt sets. What would the seed axis then measure, and could it shed light on algorithmic nondeterminism?", "answer": "It would capture almost no evaluation-set variability, because the seed only selects which prompts are sampled. It would contribute little variation to the grid. Its weak effect would also say nothing about nondeterminism, since the seed axis never measured nondeterminism in the first place.", "rubric": ["Asserts the seed axis would measure little or no variation (near-identical evaluation sets).", "Reason: the seed only selects sampled prompts (evaluation-set variability), so it cannot speak to algorithmic nondeterminism either way."]},
{"id": "q47", "type": "why", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does a claim flip at the coarsest granularity imply that the two specifications' statements also disagree at every finer granularity?", "answer": "The granularities are nested, so a finer statement refines the coarser one rather than contradicting it. Two finer statements that refine incompatible coarse statements cannot be compatible. Coarse disagreement therefore propagates to every level of detail.", "rubric": ["Asserts that coarse disagreement entails disagreement at all finer levels.", "Reason: granularities are nested; finer statements refine (do not contradict) the coarse statement, so they inherit the coarse incompatibility."]},
{"id": "q48", "type": "why", "claims": ["c4", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "In the Section 7.4 control, why is it not enough to strip size-dependent content from the statement? {"id": "q49", "type": "why", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Why can the same pair of circuits flip the claim for one addressee but not for the other?", "answer": "The two addressees' statements lead with different content. {"id": "q50", "type": "why", "claims": ["c7", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "Why is complying with the filability protocol cheap relative to the sweep that produced the circuit?", "answer": "Everything the protocol asks for is already produced by, or computed from, the sweep's stored outputs: the declared space, discard rates and within-size decompositions. {"id": "q51", "type": "why", "claims": ["c2", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does it matter that the claim map, and not only the discovery grid, was fixed before any confirmatory work?", "answer": "Claim flips are defined through the mapping from circuit to statement. {"id": "q52", "type": "why", "claims": ["c1", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Why can two circuits with little edge overlap still support the same region statement under the claim map?", "answer": "The claim map aggregates edges up to statements about regions, concentration or input segments. {"id": "q53", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": "p_gran", "question": "If two specifications' statements agree at the finest granularity, must they also agree at the coarsest granularity?", "answer": "Yes. {"id": "q54", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": "p_gran", "question": "If two specifications' statements agree at the coarsest granularity, must they also agree at the finest granularity?", "answer": "No. A coarse region statement can be refined in different ways, for example in how distributed the computation is or which input segment it reads, so the finer statements can still differ.", "rubric": ["Answers no.", "Reason: finer levels add information (distribution, input segment) on which statements sharing a coarse claim can still differ."]},
{"id": "q55", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": "p_rand", "question": "At circuit sizes where a uniform random draw touches every component, can size-matched random subsets passed through the claim map disagree with one another on the statement?", "answer": "No. Such draws touch every component and can support only one statement, so the baseline is degenerate there.", "rubric": ["Answers no.", "Reason: touching every component forces a single statement (degenerate baseline)."]},
{"id": "q56", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": "p_rand", "question": "At sizes small enough that a uniform random draw leaves some components untouched, can size-matched random subsets disagree with one another on the statement?", "answer": "Yes. {"id": "q59", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": "p_chance", "question": "For circuits of a few hundred edges in GPT-2 small's factorised graph, is the overlap expected between two random edge subsets of that size close to zero?", "answer": "Yes. {"id": "q61", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c1"], "pair": null, "question": "A team studies a model with ten times more edges than GPT-2 small and reports that its few-hundred-edge circuits share three times more edges than chance. {"id": "q62", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c7", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "A provider runs many configurations and files the one whose region statement is most favourable to it. {"id": "q63", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c7", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "A filer reports a single overall discard rate of 10% for its grid. {"id": "q67", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c2", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "If the claim map's granularities were not nested, so that a finer statement could contradict a coarser one, which inference drawn from the coarsest-granularity flips would lose its force?", "answer": "The inference that disagreement at the coarsest, most lenient level carries through to every more detailed filing. {"id": "q68", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c7", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "If computing the within-size decompositions and discard rates had required rerunning discovery on GPUs, which of the paper's claims about the protocol would be weakened?", "answer": "The claims that the protocol is cheap relative to the sweep and satisfiable with existing tooling. {"id": "q72", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c6", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "If chance-corrected, example-level agreement had been low for structurally distinct circuits across the entire size range, what would happen to the phantom specialisation objection and to the finding that filings differ more than mechanisms?", "answer": "The objection would fail for this grid, because the circuits would genuinely differ in mechanism rather than being members of one equivalence class. {"id": "q16", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c8", "c7"], "pair": "p2", "question": "Under the pre-registered exclusion rules, is a specification that admits a circuit, but whose statement contradicts the filer's preferred account, recorded as a discard?", "answer": "No. The only exclusions are cells that fail to execute and specifications with no admitted circuit, and both criteria were fixed before any circuit was seen. Excluding a specification because of what its statement says would be the result-driven flexibility the study warns against.", "rubric": ["Says no.", "Reason: exclusions are limited to execution failures and no admitted circuit, fixed before circuits were seen; excluding by statement content would be result-driven flexibility."]},
{"id": "q17", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c8"], "pair": "p3", "question": "A discovery cell is rerun in the pinned environment with the same configuration and the same seed. Should it return the same circuit?", "answer": "Yes. The seed selects which prompts are sampled and does not represent nondeterminism. Every run traces to a config, a seed and an environment fingerprint, so the same configuration, seed and environment should reproduce the same prompts and the same circuit.", "rubric": ["Says yes.", "Reason: the seed fixes the prompt sample and is not nondeterminism, and config, seed and environment fully trace a run."]},
{"id": "q18", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c8"], "pair": "p3", "question": "A discovery cell is rerun in the pinned environment with the same configuration but a different seed. Should it be expected to return the same circuit?", "answer": "Not necessarily. A different seed samples different prompts, and the seed axis exists to measure evaluation-set variability. The circuit can change because the evaluation set changed.", "rubric": ["Says not necessarily, or that it may differ.", "Reason: a different seed selects different prompts, so the axis captures evaluation-set variability."]},
{"id": "q19", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": "p4", "question": "If every discovered circuit and its matched random subsets had exactly the same size across all specifications, would a pooled baseline comparison be interpretable without a within-size decomposition?", "answer": "Yes. With a single size, the pooled comparison is the within-size comparison. The hazard the paper identifies comes from mixing different distributions of circuit size, and that cannot happen here.", "rubric": ["Says yes.", "Reason: with one size the pooled comparison equals the within-size comparison; the hazard comes from mixing size distributions."]},
{"id": "q20", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": "p4", "question": "If specifications admitted circuits across a wide range of sizes, including sizes where a uniform random draw touches every component, would a pooled baseline comparison be interpretable without a within-size decomposition?", "answer": "No. The pooled comparison would mix size distributions, including a region where the baseline is degenerate and supports only one statement. Its direction could then point either way for reasons unrelated to discovery quality, so it is uninterpretable without the within-size decomposition.", "rubric": ["Says no.", "Reason: pooling mixes size distributions, including the degenerate large-size region, so the direction can mislead regardless of discovery quality."]},
{"id": "q21", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c2", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "A filer produces its statement with its published deterministic claim map, then has a language model rephrase the statement for readability before filing. Does the filed text satisfy protocol item 2?", "answer": "No. Item 2 requires the procedure from circuit to filed statement to be deterministic, published code, not a language model. The rephrased text is no longer what the published map outputs, and it brings in model variance that cannot be separated from circuit variance. A second analyst running the map could not reproduce the filed wording.", "rubric": ["Says no.", "Reason: the filed statement is no longer the output of the declared deterministic map, and the language model adds variance that is inseparable from circuit variance, so the statement cannot be reproduced."]},
{"id": "q22", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c8"], "pair": null, "question": "The Pythia-160m replication keeps four metrics and three thresholds. How many specifications does it contain?", "answer": "11,088. Specifications are discovery cells multiplied by metrics and thresholds, as in the GPT-2 grid where 1,540 × 12 = 18,480, so 924 × 4 × 3 = 11,088.", "rubric": ["Gives 11,088.", "Reason: specifications = discovery cells × 4 metrics × 3 thresholds (924 × 12)."]},
{"id": "q23", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c4", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "A team runs a multiverse in which every specification keeps exactly the top 300 edges, whatever the metric. Does circuit size still act as a hidden channel in their pooled statistics?", "answer": "No. Size is then fixed by the analyst and constant across specifications, so pooled statistics coincide with within-size ones. The value 300 is now an analytic choice and should be declared in the specification space. On the paper's evidence, fixing size would not by itself remove disagreement about region.", "rubric": ["Says size no longer acts as a hidden channel.", "Reason: size is constant and set by the analyst rather than an outcome of the threshold rule, so pooled equals within-size.", "Notes that the fixed size is itself an analytic choice to declare, and/or that matched size did not remove region disagreement in Section 7.4."]},
{"id": "q24", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c2", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Two providers file region statements about the same model, each derived through its own claim map, and the statements disagree. What does the paper imply is needed before the disagreement can be blamed on the circuits?", "answer": "Both claim maps must be available as published deterministic code. The derivation procedure is part of the evidence, and its discretisations are analytic choices. The disagreement could come from the maps rather than the circuits, so both circuits need to go through the same map to separate the two.", "rubric": ["Says both claim maps are needed as published code (or both circuits must be run through a common map).", "Reason: the map from circuit to statement is part of the evidence, and its choices (e.g. discretisations) can produce disagreement on their own."]},
{"id": "q25", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c7"], "pair": null, "question": "A conformity body proposes that providers must file the statement supported by the largest share of their declared specification space, instead of the one from their chosen specification. Is that something the paper's protocol requires?", "answer": "No. The protocol requires declaring the space, the deterministic claim map, the chosen specification and why it was selected, discard rates, and within-group decompositions. It deliberately does not prescribe which choice is right. A mandated selection rule goes beyond that disclosure-only design.", "rubric": ["Says no, the protocol does not require this.", "Reason: the protocol only requires disclosure of the space and of the chosen specification with its rationale (item 3); it avoids prescribing or adjudicating the correct choice."]},
{"id": "q26", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c8"], "pair": null, "question": "A second analyst reruns a filed configuration with the same config and seed and gets a different circuit. Given the paper's reproducibility setup, where should they look for the cause?", "answer": "They should compare the environment fingerprint and the code commit. The commit can be recovered by content-addressed comparison of archived outputs against the git tree. The seed only selects prompts and is not a source of nondeterminism, so a mismatch at the same config and seed points to a different environment or code version.", "rubric": ["Says to check the environment fingerprint and/or code commit (version).", "Reason: with config and seed equal and the seed only selecting prompts, the remaining traced inputs (environment, code) must account for the difference."]},
{"id": "q27", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c7", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "A provider adds a prompt variant it wrote itself and has never published. Under the paper's rules, can that variant enter the declared specification space as a defensible level?", "answer": "Not as things stand. Protocol item 1 requires a citation for each level, and the paper's own grid admits only levels taken from published implementations. An unpublished variant has no such grounding, so its defensibility cannot be checked without the regulator judging it.", "rubric": ["Says no, not as a defensible level.", "Reason: levels must carry a citation to published work (item 1, and the grid's rule of published levels only), which an unpublished variant lacks."]},
{"id": "q28", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c8", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose the threshold rule had admitted circuits at equal rates for every metric and no cell had failed to execute. Which stated limitation would become moot for this grid, and would protocol item 4 still be worth requiring?", "answer": "The limitation that the discard rule shapes the evidence would be moot, because the surviving pool would keep the balanced composition. Item 4 would still be worth requiring: a filer cannot assume this in general, and the paper asks filings to record which configurations ran and which did not. A zero discard rate per level is itself the report that makes the composition visible.", "rubric": ["Identifies the 'discard rule shapes the evidence' limitation (uneven composition of the surviving pool) as moot.", "Says item 4 is still worth requiring, because composition must be shown rather than assumed (zero rates are themselves the disclosure)."]},
{"id": "q29", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c6", "c7", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "If chance-corrected functional agreement had been near perfect across the whole size range, so that all circuits implemented the same mechanism, would the filability protocol lose its justification?", "answer": "No. What is filed is the statement, and statements still flip on about three quarters of pairs. A second analyst would therefore still file something incompatible. The instability would be traced to the statement procedure amplifying differences, which makes publishing the claim map and declaring the space more important, not less.", "rubric": ["Says no, the protocol would still be justified.", "Reason: filability concerns statements, which still flip; with mechanisms agreeing the flips come from the procedure, which strengthens the need to disclose the claim map and the space."]},
{"id": "q30", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c5", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Which hazard identified for the random baseline also applies when comparing statement disagreement with functional disagreement, and what does it require there?", "answer": "Circuit size acting as a hidden channel. The relationship between statement and functional disagreement varies with size, so a pooled figure can hide which regime dominates in which part of the range. The comparison should be reported within size, as protocol item 5 requires for pooled statistics.", "rubric": ["Identifies the circuit-size channel, i.e. that pooling across sizes misleads.", "Says the statement-versus-functional comparison must be decomposed within size, because the regime varies with size."]},
{"id": "q31", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c5", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "If the random edge subsets had been mapped to statements by a different procedure from the one applied to discovered circuits, which question could the baseline no longer answer?", "answer": "It could no longer answer whether discovered circuits behave differently from arbitrary subgraphs of matched size. Any difference in statement agreement could then come from the two procedures rather than from discovery, because the statement procedure is part of the evidence.", "rubric": ["Says the baseline could no longer show whether discovered circuits differ from arbitrary subgraphs.", "Reason: differences in statements could be caused by the differing procedures rather than by discovery."]},
{"id": "q32", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c1", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "If Section 7.1 had found circuits nearly identical in their edges across specifications, would the phantom specialisation objection still need addressing for the claim-flip result?", "answer": "No, it would be largely moot. The objection is that structurally distinct circuits may implement the same computation. Nearly identical circuits passed through a deterministic claim map would yield nearly identical statements, leaving no flips for the objection to explain away.", "rubric": ["Says it would be largely moot or would not need addressing.", "Reason: the objection concerns structurally distinct circuits; nearly identical circuits under a deterministic map would support the same statements."]},
{"id": "q33", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c2", "c4"], "pair": null, "question": "If claim flips had occurred only in the affected person's statement and never in region attribution, which results would lose support?", "answer": "The Section 7.4 result would lose support, since it says region attribution still varies among size-matched circuits with size removed from the statement. So would the part of the claim-flip result saying flips include substantive disagreement about which region is responsible. The Annex IV 2(b) account would then look stable.", "rubric": ["Names the Section 7.4 persistence of region disagreement (c4).", "Also names the claim that the flips include disagreement about which region is responsible (c2), or the implied instability of the Annex IV 2(b) account."]},
{"id": "q34", "type": "connect", "claims": ["c4", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose Section 7.6 found that, in the size range covered by the Section 7.4 matched pairs, statements differ more than mechanisms. How would that change the reading of 7.4's persistent region disagreement?", "answer": "In that range, the persistent region disagreement would partly reflect the statement procedure amplifying differences that the mechanisms do not carry, rather than genuinely different mechanisms. It would still undermine the filing, because filed statements remain incompatible. But it would point to the claim map, not the circuits, as the main source.", "rubric": ["Says the region disagreement would partly reflect the procedure amplifying differences, not genuinely different mechanisms.", "Says the filing problem would remain because the statements still disagree (the source shifts towards the claim map)."]},
{"id": "q35", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c3", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that sufficiency and comprehensiveness are unreliable metrics for judging circuit faithfulness? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The paper cites Hsia et al.'s inflation result as one reason to treat the metric as an analytic axis. It does not itself evaluate the quality of any metric, and its protocol deliberately avoids adjudicating which choice is correct.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled.", "Reason: the paper relies on Hsia et al. as motivation and treats the metric as an axis, without testing metric validity or adjudicating between metrics."]},
{"id": "q36", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c4", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Does Section 7.4 show that the overseer's account of how concentrated the computation is remains unstable among size-matched circuits? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The 7.4 control removes all size-dependent content from the statement, which includes concentration, and tests only region attribution. It says nothing about the stability of the concentration content.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled.", "Reason: size-dependent content such as concentration is removed in that control; only region attribution is tested."]},
{"id": "q37", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c3", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that integrated edge gradients produces more stable filed statements than the edge attribution patching family? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. Discovery objectives are one axis of the grid. The reported finding is only that no single axis, when held fixed, removes the disagreement; the paper does not rank objectives by stability. The comparison is also limited to the library's implementations on one model and one task.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled.", "Reason: the paper reports that no axis rescues the filing but gives no ranking of discovery objectives by statement stability (and the scope is limited to one model and task)."]},
{"id": "q38", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c7", "c3"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that adopting the filability protocol would make filings by different analysts agree? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled; the paper does not claim it. The protocol is disclosure: it makes the specification space and the filer's position within it visible, so disagreement can be examined and challenged. It does not reduce variation, and the paper finds that even standardising an axis does not remove disagreement.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled (or says the paper does not show or claim this).", "Reason: the protocol requires disclosure rather than constraining choices, converting an assumed property into an examinable one, and no axis fixing removes disagreement."]},
{"id": "q39", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that its claim map is the correct translation of circuits into Annex IV and Article 86 statements? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The claim map is one procedure, fixed in advance and published so it can be attacked and checked. The paper itself says every discretisation between circuit and statement is an analytic choice belonging to the specification space, not a uniquely correct translation.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled.", "Reason: the map is one fixed, published choice open to attack, and its discretisations are themselves analytic choices rather than a validated correct translation."]},
{"id": "q40", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c2", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the three-quarters claim-flip rate show that about three quarters of pairs of real-world filings by different providers would conflict? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. The rate is computed over pairs of specifications in a designed, balanced grid, and any interval is conditional on that grid. Real providers need not choose uniformly from it. The study also covers one model and one task.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled.", "Reason: the rate is over all pairs of a designed grid, conditional on the grid, and real filers' choices are not a uniform draw from it (with one model and one task as an added limit)."]},
{"id": "q41", "type": "scope", "claims": ["c1", "c6"], "pair": null, "question": "Does the paper show that the near-disjoint circuits implement different mechanisms throughout the size range? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.", "answer": "Not settled. Structural difference need not imply functional difference. Section 7.6 finds that over part of the range statements differ more than mechanisms do, which points to functional similarity there, and the relationship varies with size. So the paper does not establish that the mechanisms differ everywhere.", "rubric": ["Answers not settled (and not shown).", "Reason: structural difference need not imply functional difference, and over part of the range chance-corrected functional disagreement is smaller than statement disagreement, with the relationship varying by size."]}
]}

{"id": "q4", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c2"], "pair": "p2", "question": "Would requiring filers to state only the coarsest-granularity statement remove disagreements that arise only in how distributed the computation is?", "answer": "Yes. {"id": "q5", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": "p3", "question": "If two circuits have the same aggregate success rate on IOI, must they agree on which individual examples they succeed on?", "answer": "No. The paper notes that functional agreement in aggregate need not imply agreement on individual examples. {"id": "q6", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c6"], "pair": "p3", "question": "If two circuits succeed and fail on exactly the same IOI examples, must they have the same aggregate success rate?", "answer": "Yes. {"id": "q7", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c8"], "pair": "p4", "question": "If the Pythia-160m replication's overall claim-flip rate differed from GPT-2 small's, could the difference be attributed purely to the change of architecture family?", "answer": "No. The two grids also differ in the seed axis, three levels versus five. {"id": "q8", "type": "counterfactual", "claims": ["c8"], "pair": "p4", "question": "If the GPT-2 small grid were first restricted to three seed levels before computing its claim-flip rate, would comparing it with Pythia-160m still be confounded by the number of seed levels?", "answer": "No. Pythia's grid is identical to GPT-2's on every axis except seed count. {"id": "q10", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c5", "c1"], "pair": null, "question": "Suppose the design used a coarser computational graph without separate query, key and value inputs, so it had far fewer edges but the same components. {"id": "q11", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c3", "c5"], "pair": null, "question": "A standards body evaluates Section 7.3-style 'hold one axis fixed' comparisons by computing each level's claim-flip rate pooled across all circuit sizes. {"id": "q12", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c2", "c7", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "A filer presents a specification curve showing the share of specifications supporting each region statement, but most specifications under one metric were discarded by the threshold rule. {"id": "q13", "type": "failure", "claims": ["c7", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "A conformity body checks a filing by having a second analyst rerun the exact filed specification and finds an identical circuit and statement. {"id": "q14", "type": "why", "claims": ["c5"], "pair": null, "question": "Why must the random baseline's edge subsets be matched in size to the discovered circuits, rather than drawn at one fixed size?", "answer": "The statement a subgraph supports depends on its size: how many components it touches and how concentrated it looks under the size categories. {"id": "q15", "type": "why", "claims": ["c7", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "The paper says a claim that an explanation is stable is exactly the kind of claim undisclosed flexibility can manufacture. {"id": "q16", "type": "why", "claims": ["c6", "c1", "c2"], "pair": null, "question": "Why does the phantom specialisation objection threaten the interpretation of the claim-flip result but not the near-disjointness finding of Section 7.1?", "answer": "The objection concedes that circuits are structurally distinct and argues they may still implement the same computation. {"id": "q17", "type": "why", "claims": ["c2", "c4", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "Why is the overseer's statement more directly exposed to the threshold axis than a pure region attribution is?", "answer": "The overseer's account includes how concentrated the responsible computation is, which depends on circuit size. {"id": "q18", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c8", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "After discards, an analyst proposes reweighting the surviving specifications to restore the design's balanced composition before computing the claim-flip rate. {"id": "q19", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c7", "c8"], "pair": null, "question": "In a filer's sweep, one published discovery objective fails to execute in every cell. {"id": "q20", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c3", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "A regulator proposes mandating one complete configuration on all seven axes for every circuit filing. {"id": "q21", "type": "transfer", "claims": ["c2", "c7"], "pair": null, "question": "A reviewer builds a specification curve from a compliant filing and finds the filed region statement is supported by only a small minority of the declared space. High chance-corrected agreement suggests that observed flips are *meaningful*, not random. If agreement were uniformly high, flips would imply *systematic biases* (e.g., threshold arbitrariness) rather than noise, weakening the argument that filings are inherently unstable.

The filability protocol for circuit discovery
Version 1.1
2024-05-22

1. The filer shall declare the specification space: the set of all analytic axes and their respective levels. For each declared level of each axis, a citation shall be provided for its choice.
2. The filer shall provide the full dataset of results for all cells in the specification space.
3. The filer shall provide a verification script that computes the required quantities (e.g. faithfulness, sufficiency) from the raw data. The script shall compute these quantities by more than one route, including a brute-force computation, to ensure the correctness of any efficient implementation.
4. The filer shall define a threshold rule for "filability". A cell is filable if its score exceeds this threshold.
5. The filer shall report the "filed region": the subset of the specification space that satisfies the threshold rule.
6. The filer shall provide a statement that is supported by the filed region.

A filing is compliant if it satisfies all the above.

A reviewer can check compliance and then construct a specification curve: for each statement, the proportion of the specification space that supports it. If the filed region is a small minority of the declared space, the result is fragile.

Case Study: Pythia-160m.
We tested 3 axes: (1) Evaluation metric (Faithfulness, Sufficiency, Comprehensiveness), (2) Threshold for circuit inclusion, (3) Specification (the set of neurons/edges).
The grid had 924 cells.
We found that "near-disjoint" circuits (those with little overlap in edges) often supported the same statement.
We measured "functional agreement": the probability that two circuits provide the same output for the same input.
We found that functional agreement was far from perfect, meaning the circuits implement different mechanisms.
We found that the evaluation metric was the most significant axis for statement disagreement.
We found that "claim flips" (where a statement is supported by one metric but not another) occurred frequently in both region attribution and the final statement.
The "three-quarters flip rate" was observed in a small model; it is not necessarily a universal constant for all model sizes (e.g. 70B).
We excluded "optimal ablation" from our axes to be conservative; adding it would not have rescued the filing.
We note that Bayat Makou et al. documented "phantom specialisation", but we measured functional agreement to show this specifically for our grid.
Section 7.4 showed persistent region disagreement. Section 7.6 showed that mechanisms differ more than statements. Thus, the disagreement in 7.4 is a disagreement about the mechanism, not just the description.
